projectTitle: Cinder Labs: The Audit That Found the Exploit First
projectTagline: A 20-video, start-to-finish smart contract build for a fictional DeFi team -- a real staking contract taken from design through Hardhat testing and a Base testnet deployment, then a genuine reentrancy vulnerability caught by an internal security audit before mainnet, not by an attacker after launch.
businessContext: Cinder Labs is building EmberStake, a staking contract for their utility token $EMBER, paying out ETH-denominated rewards from a share of protocol fees. Vivian Castellan (Head of Product) wants real, revenue-generating staking live on mainnet -- but only if it's actually safe, since a smart contract holding real funds can't be patched the way a server can. Desmond Okoro (Smart Contract Engineer) builds the contract and its test suite; Naomi Fitzwilliam (Security Lead) runs the dedicated pre-mainnet audit that finds a real reentrancy vulnerability in the rewards-claiming function -- one the happy-path test suite was never going to catch, because it only ever tested normal wallets, never a malicious contract.
architectureSummary: EmberStake.sol, written in Solidity on OpenZeppelin base contracts, tracks staked $EMBER balances and ETH-denominated reward balances, deployed to Base (an Ethereum L2) via Base Sepolia testnet first. Hardhat handles development and testing; Slither handles static analysis as part of a dedicated internal security audit; a Node.js/TypeScript indexer and REST API expose on-chain state to the frontend. The real defect wasn't in the staking logic itself -- it was in claimRewards(), which sent a user's ETH reward before zeroing their reward balance, a checks-effects-interactions violation that let a malicious contract re-enter the function and drain the shared reward pool in a single transaction.

lessons.title: Meeting Cinder Labs: A Staking Contract That Has to Survive Mainnet
lessons.summary: The discovery meeting: Cinder Labs wants $EMBER holders to stake their tokens for real ETH rewards -- and the contract holding that money can't be patched after launch the way a server can. What Desmond Okoro has to learn before a line of Solidity gets written.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Over the next 20 videos, you'll walk through one complete, start-to-finish smart-contract build for a real DeFi feature at a fictional crypto-native team, **Cinder Labs**. Cinder Labs already has a working, already-deployed ERC-20 token, **$EMBER** -- this series does not build the token itself. What it doesn't have yet is a way for $EMBER holders to actually stake those tokens and earn something real for locking them up: a share of the protocol's own fee revenue, paid out in ETH.

That feature has a name before it has any code: **EmberStake**. Users will deposit $EMBER into it and, in return, earn ETH-denominated rewards drawn from a share of protocol fees. It sounds like a fairly ordinary feature request. What makes it genuinely different is the thing every smart-contract team has to internalize before writing a single line: once EmberStake is deployed to a real blockchain holding real user funds, there is no server to SSH into and no hotfix to ship if something is wrong. A bug discovered after real money is locked inside the contract is a very different kind of emergency than a bug in a web app.

You are **Desmond Okoro**, the Smart Contract Engineer building EmberStake end to end. This video starts exactly where a responsible build like this has to start: not with `EmberStake.sol`, not with a Hardhat project, but with a meeting where you find out from the business side what "ship real staking, safely" actually means, who's accountable for which piece, and what's genuinely at stake if this goes wrong on mainnet.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a school is going to put a real coin-operated vending machine out on the sidewalk, except this machine is special: once it's bolted down and switched on, nobody -- not even the kids who built it -- can open it back up to fix a mistake. If a kid programmed it wrong and it hands out two candies for every coin instead of one, that mistake just keeps happening, to everyone who uses it, until all the candy is gone. There's no quick fix once the machine is sealed and sitting on the sidewalk.

That's what Cinder Labs is building with EmberStake, except instead of candy, it's real money. People will put their $EMBER tokens into it and expect to earn real ETH back over time. Before any of that gets built, Desmond has to sit down with the people in charge and understand exactly what "done safely" means -- because once this machine is bolted to the sidewalk, there's no taking it back inside to fix.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The detail that matters most in this discovery meeting is not the feature description -- "users stake $EMBER and earn ETH" is simple enough to fit on a product one-pager. What matters is getting precise about why this specific kind of software carries a risk profile unlike almost anything else a typical engineering team ships: deployed contract bytecode is, for all practical purposes, immutable. There's no server to patch, no container to redeploy with a fix, and no way to quietly roll back a bad transaction once it's confirmed on-chain. A defect that would be an annoying bug ticket in a web application becomes, in a staking contract, a direct and often irreversible loss of real user funds and real ETH.

Four people matter in this discovery conversation, and each owns a different piece of what "safe" has to mean. **Vivian Castellan**, Head of Product, is the business sponsor -- her stated goal is real, revenue-generating staking live on mainnet, and her stated worry, the one that should anchor every requirement that follows, is whether this is actually safe to put real money behind. **Desmond Okoro** is the engineer who will design and implement `EmberStake.sol` itself. **Naomi Fitzwilliam**, Security Lead, will later run a dedicated internal security audit of the finished contract -- including a genuine attempt to break it -- before any of it touches mainnet; she isn't needed to find anything yet, but her role in the process has to be established now, not invented after the fact once code already exists. **Julian Hargrove**, Backend/Infrastructure Engineer, will build the Node.js/TypeScript indexer and REST API that lets a frontend show real staking stats by listening to the contract's on-chain events -- his piece depends entirely on what events and state Desmond's contract actually exposes, which is itself a reason this has to be planned, not improvised.

Getting the real shape of the ask right now -- $EMBER staking in, ETH rewards out, a genuine audit gate before mainnet -- is what keeps every later requirement in this series honest about what Cinder Labs is actually asking for, instead of what merely sounds reasonable in isolation.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Walk in already knowing what you don't know

Before the meeting, write down what you need to confirm, not just what you expect to hear:

- Is $EMBER really already deployed and live, or does any part of the token itself still need building?
- Where does the ETH that pays rewards actually come from -- a real share of protocol fees, or something that still needs defining?
- Does anything about staking or rewards need to work the moment this ships, or is there room to build this carefully?

## Step 2 -- Run the meeting and get the real ask in Vivian Castellan's own words

```
VIVIAN:    Here's the real ask. $EMBER is already live -- people hold
           it, trade it, nothing about the token itself needs to
           change. What we don't have is a reason to actually hold
           it. I want people to be able to stake $EMBER and earn
           real ETH back, a share of what the protocol actually
           earns in fees. Real revenue-sharing, live on mainnet.

DESMOND:   And what's the thing you're actually worried about?

VIVIAN:    Honestly? Whether this is actually safe to put real money
           behind. This isn't a website where we patch a bug
           Tuesday morning. If we get this wrong with real funds
           locked inside it, there's no taking it back.
```

## Step 3 -- Ask Naomi Fitzwilliam what "safe" has to mean here

```
DESMOND:   Naomi, when this is ready, what does your side of this
           actually look like?

NAOMI:     Before a single dollar of real user funds touches
           mainnet, I run a dedicated internal security audit on the
           finished contract -- and that includes me genuinely
           trying to exploit it, not just reading the code and
           nodding. If I find something, it gets fixed and I check
           again. That gate doesn't move for a launch date.

DESMOND:   Good -- I'd rather hear that now than assume it later.
```

## Step 4 -- Ask Julian Hargrove what he needs from the contract

```
DESMOND:   Julian, what do you actually need from me to build the
           indexer and API?

JULIAN:    Real on-chain events I can listen to -- when someone
           stakes, when someone withdraws, when someone claims
           rewards. If the contract doesn't emit the right events
           with the right data, I can't show accurate staking stats
           on the frontend no matter how good my API is. That's
           worth us agreeing on early, not after you've already
           written the contract.
```

## Step 5 -- Confirm the real shape of EmberStake

```
EMBERSTAKE -- WHAT VIVIAN IS ACTUALLY ASKING FOR

Action            What happens                          Tracked in
stake(amount)     User deposits $EMBER via               stakedBalance
                  transferFrom
withdraw(amount)  User gets staked $EMBER back            stakedBalance
claimRewards()    User claims real ETH, a share of        rewardBalance
                  protocol fees

Token:        $EMBER -- an existing, already-deployed ERC-20. Not
              rebuilt in this project.
Rewards:      Paid in ETH, not more $EMBER.
Gate:         A real internal security audit, run by Naomi
              Fitzwilliam, before any real funds are exposed on
              mainnet.
```

## Step 6 -- Write the discovery summary and confirm it with Vivian

```
CINDER LABS -- DISCOVERY SUMMARY

Business problem:   $EMBER holders have no reason to hold the token
                    beyond speculation. Cinder Labs wants a staking
                    contract, EmberStake, that pays real ETH rewards
                    from a share of protocol fees -- live on
                    mainnet, holding real user funds.
Sponsor:            Vivian Castellan, Head of Product.
Key roles:          Desmond Okoro (Smart Contract Engineer, builds
                    EmberStake.sol), Naomi Fitzwilliam (Security
                    Lead, runs the audit before mainnet), Julian
                    Hargrove (Backend/Infrastructure Engineer, builds
                    the indexer/API off the contract's events).
Open question:      Is this actually safe to put real money behind?
                    Nothing in this project gets to assume "yes"
                    until Naomi's audit says so.
```

Send this summary to Vivian Castellan and ask directly: "Did I capture this accurately?" Every requirement written in the next lesson traces back to a line in this document -- and her sign-off on the real ask is what keeps that requirement honest about what actually needs to be true before this goes live.

lessons.title: Turning 'Ship It Safely' Into a Testable Requirement
lessons.summary: Converting Vivian Castellan's 'ship it safely' into one precise, testable requirement: EmberStake must correctly track staked and reward balances under real usage and under adversarial conditions, and must pass a dedicated internal security audit -- including a real attempt to exploit it -- before a single dollar of real user funds touches mainnet.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Discovery gave you a real ask and an honest picture of what Cinder Labs actually needs -- but "ship it safely" isn't a requirement yet, it's an intention. This lesson turns that intention into one precise, written requirement you can actually design against and, eventually, test.

The requirement has two parts. First, EmberStake must correctly track every staker's balances -- $EMBER tracked in `stakedBalance`, ETH rewards tracked in `rewardBalance` -- not just under normal, well-behaved usage, but under adversarial conditions: someone actively trying to manipulate the contract into paying out rewards twice, withdrawing more $EMBER than they ever staked, or otherwise draining funds that aren't theirs. Second, and just as important, EmberStake must pass a dedicated internal security audit, run by Naomi Fitzwilliam, that includes an explicit, genuine attempt to exploit the contract -- before a single dollar of real user $EMBER or real ETH rewards is exposed on mainnet. Whether EmberStake, once built, actually lives up to that standard is something this series has to verify honestly later -- not something to assume solved just because the requirement sounds right on paper. Whether this contract is actually safe to put real money behind stays the open question driving the rest of this series.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine the two kids running the vending machine finally agree their machine needs a real plan before it goes outside. "Make it safe" doesn't tell anyone what to actually build or check. So they get specific: the machine has to give back the right amount of candy and the right change no matter what -- even if someone tries putting in fake coins, or mashing the buttons in a weird order to trick it into giving out candy twice. And before it ever goes outside for real, a mechanic who didn't build it has to come try to break it on purpose, specifically looking for ways to cheat it -- not just glance at it and say it looks fine.

That's the requirement for EmberStake. It has to track everyone's deposits and rewards correctly, even when someone is actively trying to cheat it, not just when everyone behaves nicely. And before real money goes anywhere near it, Naomi has to genuinely try to break it herself -- and it has to survive that, every time.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A requirement that can't be falsified isn't a requirement, it's a hope -- and "ship it safely" is exactly that until it's pinned to a precise correctness standard and a precise audit gate.

The correctness half has to go beyond the happy path on purpose. It would be easy to write a test suite that stakes some $EMBER, waits, claims some rewards, withdraws, and calls it done -- and that tells you almost nothing about whether EmberStake is actually safe. The real risk lives in adversarial behavior: can someone call `claimRewards()` twice for the same reward period and get paid twice? Can someone call `withdraw()` for more than their own `stakedBalance`? Can the order or timing of calls be manipulated to drain funds that belong to other stakers? This requirement commits, in writing, to an automated test suite that includes deliberate adversarial cases, not only normal ones.

The audit half deserves equal weight, because it's the one most likely to get quietly treated as a formality once a deadline is close. Naomi Fitzwilliam's internal security audit is defined here as a real gate: it includes a genuine, hands-on attempt to exploit the deployed-candidate contract, and a finding from that attempt blocks mainnet deployment until it's fixed and re-checked -- the same way a failing test blocks a merge. This requirement does not yet claim EmberStake, once built, will actually pass that audit cleanly. It commits Cinder Labs, in writing, to the standard the rest of this series is building toward, and to testing that standard honestly once real code exists -- not assuming it's met because the right words appear in a requirements document.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Pull the real constraint out of Vivian's side of the business

```
DESMOND:   You said "ship it safely" in the first meeting. What
           would actually have to be true for you to call that
           delivered?

VIVIAN:    Two things. First, I need to know the contract actually
           tracks everyone's $EMBER and everyone's ETH rewards
           correctly -- not just when people use it normally, but
           when someone is actively trying to cheat it. Second, I
           need Naomi to genuinely try to break it before any real
           money goes anywhere near mainnet, and I need that to
           actually block launch if she finds something.

DESMOND:   Can you say more about the first part? What's "someone
           trying to cheat it" actually look like to you?

VIVIAN:    I don't know the exact attack. That's your and Naomi's
           job to think through. What I know is I don't want to find
           out the hard way, with real user funds already locked in
           it.
```

## Step 2 -- Ask Naomi Fitzwilliam what "adversarial" means in practice

```
DESMOND:   Naomi, when you eventually audit this, what kinds of
           things are you actually going to try?

NAOMI:     Real attempts to break it, not a checklist read-through.
           Can I claim the same rewards twice? Can I withdraw more
           $EMBER than I actually staked? Can I manipulate the order
           of calls to drain someone else's balance? If I find a
           real way to do any of that, it's not a nitpick -- it
           blocks mainnet until Desmond fixes it and I check again.
```

## Step 3 -- Fix the exact requirement in writing

```
REQUIREMENT -- EMBERSTAKE SHIP IT SAFELY (V1)

REQ-1: EmberStake.sol must correctly track every staker's
       stakedBalance and rewardBalance under real usage AND under
       adversarial conditions -- including attempts to double-claim
       rewards, withdraw more than was staked, or otherwise drain
       funds that aren't the caller's -- verified by an automated
       test suite that includes deliberate adversarial test cases,
       not only normal ones.
REQ-2: EmberStake must pass a dedicated internal security audit, run
       by Naomi Fitzwilliam, including an explicit, genuine attempt
       to exploit the contract -- before a single dollar of real
       user $EMBER or real ETH rewards is exposed on mainnet. A
       finding from that attempt blocks mainnet deployment until
       it's fixed and re-audited.
```

## Step 4 -- Say out loud what this requirement doesn't promise yet

```
DESMOND:   I want to be clear about one thing. REQ-1 and REQ-2 are
           the standard -- correct under attack, and a real audit
           gate before mainnet. They're not yet a claim that
           EmberStake, once built, actually meets that standard.
           That's real implementation and audit work still ahead,
           and I want Naomi to check it honestly once the contract
           exists, not assume it's fine because we wrote it down.

VIVIAN:    That's fair -- I just need to know that's the bar we're
           actually building toward, and that someone really checks
           it before this touches real money.
```

## Step 5 -- Sanity-check the requirement against a real scenario

```
Scenario: A staker calls claimRewards() and, before that transaction
          finishes updating their rewardBalance, finds a way to call
          claimRewards() again and get paid a second time for the
          same rewards. Under REQ-1, this has to be impossible and
          has to be caught by the adversarial test suite -- and
          under REQ-2, it's exactly the kind of thing Naomi's audit
          is designed to find before mainnet, not after.
```

Walk this scenario past Vivian and Naomi directly and ask: "Is this exactly the kind of thing you mean by 'safe'?"

## Step 6 -- Get the requirement signed off

Save REQ-1 and REQ-2 alongside the Lesson 1 discovery summary. Get explicit sign-off from Vivian Castellan on REQ-2 specifically -- the audit-as-a-real-gate standard is the line most likely to get quietly softened later, once a launch date is close and the contract looks like it's working fine in normal use.

Vivian has signed off in writing, which is what every later design and implementation decision in this project gets measured against.

lessons.title: Scoping V1: One Staking Contract and a Real Audit
lessons.summary: Drawing a hard line around what V1 actually ships -- EmberStake.sol, its test suite, a real internal security audit, an indexer/API, and a mainnet deployment -- and naming what's explicitly deferred: an NFT marketplace, a DAO governance system, and rebuilding $EMBER itself.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
You now have a precise, signed-off requirement. Before any Solidity file gets written, this lesson draws a hard written line around what V1 of this build actually delivers -- and, just as importantly, what it explicitly does not. For Cinder Labs, V1 ships five things: the `EmberStake.sol` staking contract itself; its automated test suite, including the adversarial cases REQ-1 demands; a dedicated internal security audit, run by Naomi Fitzwilliam, including a genuine attempt to exploit the contract; the Node.js/TypeScript indexer and REST API Julian Hargrove builds around the contract's on-chain events; and, once the audit passes, a real deployment to mainnet.

What's explicitly out of scope, named in writing rather than left to assumption, is anything beyond that staking core. This project does not build an **NFT marketplace** -- a real, valuable idea at Cinder Labs, deliberately deferred and named rather than quietly dropped. It does not build a **DAO governance system** -- also real, also deferred, also a different project with a different scope. And it does not rebuild or redesign **$EMBER** itself -- the token stays exactly as it already exists, already deployed; EmberStake's job is to let people stake it and earn rewards against it, not to change what it is.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine the two kids running the vending machine finally get real help: a grown-up agrees to build them one proper, safe machine, with a real plan for testing it and a mechanic who checks it before it ever goes outside. A good helper like that does one job well: build one safe machine, test it hard, and have it checked by someone trying to break it. A helper who also tried to build a second, totally different machine that trades trading cards, or set up a whole voting system for the kids to decide things together, while also still trying to finish the first machine, would be doing a much bigger job than anyone actually asked for -- and the one machine that actually matters right now might never get finished properly.

This project is that real helper, doing exactly the first job well. It builds one staking machine, tests it hard, and gets it checked -- it doesn't build a trading-card machine or a voting system at the same time, and it doesn't touch the coins people already have.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Scope discipline matters here specifically because a working staking contract is an unusually tempting foundation to build on top of once it exists. The moment EmberStake is live, tracking real balances and paying real rewards, it's natural for stakeholders to ask "can we also launch an NFT collection off this?" or "should we let stakers vote on protocol decisions while we're in here?" Both are reasonable product ideas, and neither belongs in V1.

An NFT marketplace is deferred because it's a genuinely separate product with its own contract design, its own marketplace mechanics, and its own audit surface -- bolting it onto EmberStake's scope would mean two different kinds of risk sharing one launch date, which serves neither well. A DAO governance system is deferred for the same reason: real on-chain governance means its own token-weighted voting logic, its own proposal and execution mechanics, and its own attack surface around vote manipulation -- a different project, worth naming now so it doesn't get lost as a vague someday, not worth building before the staking contract it would presumably govern even exists safely. And rebuilding $EMBER itself is out of scope for the clearest reason of all: it's an existing, already-deployed, already-trusted ERC-20 token -- EmberStake's entire job is to be a contract that other contracts and users interact with by holding and transferring $EMBER as it already works today, not a reason to touch the token's own code.

What V1 commits to is narrower and fully ownable: one staking contract, one real audit, one indexer/API, one mainnet deployment -- not a second product, not a governance system, and not a token rewrite.

## Step 4 -- Rehearse the scope-creep conversation before it happens

```
           own audit from scratch. I'd rather name it now as a
           future initiative than fold it into this audit and risk
           neither one getting the real scrutiny it needs.
```

## Step 5 -- Get written sign-off from Vivian and Naomi

Attach this scope document to the Lesson 1 and Lesson 2 artifacts and ask both directly: "Do you agree the NFT marketplace, DAO governance, and any change to $EMBER itself are out of scope for V1?" That's the line most likely to get reinterpreted later, once a working staking contract exists and looks easy to extend.

## Step 6 -- Treat the deferred list as a real backlog, not a dead end

Naming the NFT marketplace and the DAO governance system as deferred, rather than simply declining them, matters for how the rest of the organization reads this decision. A deferred item has an owner, a rough rationale, and a place it can resurface once V1 has actually shipped and proven itself; a silently dropped idea tends to come back later as a surprise, re-argued from scratch, often at a worse time. Desmond keeps both items in the same written record as the V1 scope statement, specifically so that when Vivian or marketing raises an NFT drop again in six months, the answer is "yes, that's still on the list, here's why it waited," not a blank look.

lessons.title: Choosing the Stack: Solidity, Hardhat, OpenZeppelin, and Base
lessons.summary: The first real architecture decision: Solidity as the contract language, OpenZeppelin's audited base contracts (including ReentrancyGuard) over hand-rolled primitives, Hardhat for development and testing, Slither for static analysis, and Base Sepolia/Base as the deployment network -- each justified against a real alternative for Cinder Labs's actual situation.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
With scope locked, this is the first real architecture decision: exactly which technologies EmberStake is built on. The stack this lesson fixes is **Solidity** as the contract language; **OpenZeppelin Contracts** as the base library EmberStake builds on, including its `ReentrancyGuard`, rather than hand-rolled equivalents; **Hardhat** for development and testing; **Slither** for static analysis as part of the security audit process; and **Base Sepolia** as the testnet for development and staging, with **Base** -- an Ethereum layer-2 -- as the mainnet network for production.

Each choice earns its place against a real alternative, not just convention. The decision this lesson spends the most time on is the network: why Base, an Ethereum L2, instead of deploying straight to Ethereum mainnet. That decision traces directly back to how $EMBER holders will actually use EmberStake -- claiming ETH rewards is something a staker might reasonably want to do often, and Ethereum mainnet gas costs can eat a meaningful share of a small, frequent reward claim in a way they wouldn't on a cheaper L2. This lesson fixes the stack. It does not yet claim the stack alone guarantees REQ-1 and REQ-2 are met -- that depends on how `EmberStake.sol` is actually written and how thoroughly it's actually tested and audited against this stack, which is real work still ahead in this series, not something to assume solved just because the right technologies were chosen.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine the grown-up helping with the vending machine now has to decide what the machine is actually built out of, and where it gets parked. They could build every single part from scratch, including the coin slot and the lock, or they could use parts that thousands of other machines already use and that mechanics have already checked over and over for ways to cheat them -- like a coin slot that's already known to be hard to trick. For a machine holding real money, using the already-checked parts is worth it, instead of reinventing a lock that might have a flaw nobody's found yet.

They also have to decide where to park the machine. Parking it right on the busiest, most expensive street in town means every single person who uses it pays a steep parking fee just to get near it -- fine if you're buying something big, annoying if you just want one piece of candy. Parking it one block over, on a nearly identical but much cheaper street that's still watched by the same police department, means people can visit it often without the fee eating up what they came for. That's why this machine gets built with already-trusted parts, and parked somewhere cheaper to visit but just as safe.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Every technology on this list traces back to a real requirement from the first three lessons, not a default stack someone copied from a tutorial.

Start with **Solidity** as the contract language. It's the dominant, most battle-tested language for EVM-compatible contracts, with by far the deepest tooling, audit experience, and hiring pool available -- an alternative like Vyper has real adherents for its deliberately restricted feature set, but for a team that needs to move efficiently through a real audit process with an auditor, Naomi Fitzwilliam, who needs mature tooling to actually do that audit, Solidity is the choice with the least unnecessary risk.

The decision that deserves the most scrutiny on the library side is choosing **OpenZeppelin Contracts** as the base EmberStake builds on, specifically including its `ReentrancyGuard`, rather than writing equivalent primitives from scratch. Reentrancy -- where an external call lets an attacker's code call back into the contract before its state finishes updating -- is one of the most common real causes of smart-contract exploits, and it's exactly the kind of subtle, order-of-operations bug REQ-1's adversarial testing standard exists to catch. OpenZeppelin's contracts have been used, reviewed, and attacked in production across a huge number of real protocols for years; a hand-rolled reentrancy guard written fresh for EmberStake would be unaudited by definition, the first time it's ever run against a real adversary. Building on an already-audited, widely-used library doesn't make EmberStake safe by itself, but it removes a whole category of risk that has nothing to do with EmberStake's own business logic, which is exactly where Naomi's audit time is better spent.

**Hardhat** is chosen for development and testing over an alternative like Foundry because of its mature JavaScript/TypeScript-based testing ecosystem and plugin support, which fits naturally with Julian Hargrove's Node.js/TypeScript indexer and API work sharing types and tooling across the same stack. **Slither**, a static analysis tool, is planned as a standing part of the audit process alongside Naomi's manual exploit attempts -- it catches a class of common Solidity pitfalls (unchecked external calls, certain reentrancy patterns, dangerous arithmetic) automatically and cheaply, before a human auditor's time goes toward the subtler business-logic issues static analysis can't see.

The network decision carries the most direct weight on the product itself. Deploying straight to Ethereum mainnet is the default assumption for a lot of DeFi protocols, but Vivian Castellan's actual stated goal is real, ongoing engagement from $EMBER holders -- staking, and presumably claiming ETH rewards, somewhat regularly. Ethereum mainnet gas costs make frequent small claims genuinely uneconomical for many holders; a reward claim that costs more in gas than the reward itself is worth defeats the entire point of the feature. **Base**, an Ethereum L2, offers materially lower transaction costs while still settling to and inheriting its security model from Ethereum -- it is not a different trust assumption, it's a cheaper lane on the same highway. **Base Sepolia** is the matching testnet, used for development and staging before anything real is at stake. None of this is itself proof that REQ-1 and REQ-2 are actually satisfied -- that depends on how `EmberStake.sol` is actually written and tested against this stack, which is real work for the implementation lessons ahead.
