lessons.title: Designing the EmberStake Contract: Staking, Rewards, and Withdrawals
lessons.summary: Designing EmberStake.sol's core data model and function surface -- the stakedBalance and rewardBalance mappings, the stake/withdraw/claimRewards signatures, and how a share of protocol fees accrues to stakers proportional to their stake -- before Desmond Okoro writes a single line of the real implementation.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Cinder Labs already has $EMBER live as a deployed ERC-20 token. What doesn't exist yet is EmberStake, the contract that lets a holder lock up $EMBER and earn a share of the protocol's ETH fee revenue in return. Before Desmond Okoro writes any Solidity, Vivian Castellan needs a clear answer to "what does this contract actually track, and what can a user do with it" -- and Desmond needs that answer nailed down before implementation starts, because changing a contract's storage layout after it's deployed is far more painful than changing a design document.

This lesson designs EmberStake.sol at the architecture level: two mappings (`stakedBalance` and `rewardBalance`), three external entry points (`stake`, `withdraw`, `claimRewards`), and the mechanism by which protocol fees turn into claimable ETH for each staker, proportional to how much $EMBER they have staked. The actual Solidity bodies for `stake` and `withdraw` get written in the implementation lesson immediately ahead; `claimRewards` and its reward math get written in the lesson after that, by a separate pass. This lesson's job is only to settle what the contract's shape has to be before any of that code gets typed.
lessons.explainSimple:
Picture a community tip jar connected to a locker room. You put your $EMBER tokens in a locker (that's staking) and you get a receipt that says how much is yours. Every so often the shop drops some tip money into the jar, and the jar splits it among everyone with a locker, based on how full their locker is compared to everyone else's. You can grab your share of the tip jar whenever you want, and you can take your tokens back out of your locker whenever you want too.

This lesson is Desmond drawing the floor plan for that locker room and tip jar before he builds either one: how many lockers, how the receipts work, and exactly how the tip-splitting math is supposed to behave. Nobody's token has moved yet.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The design settles on two mappings scoped to `address`: `stakedBalance` for principal (how much $EMBER a given address currently has locked in the contract) and `rewardBalance` for already-accrued, claimable ETH owed to that address. A third piece of state, `totalStaked`, tracks the sum of all principal and is required by the reward math below.

Rewards are specified as a share of protocol fees distributed proportionally to stake, which Desmond designs as a reward-per-token accumulator -- the same shape used by Synthetix's `StakingRewards` and now something of a standard pattern for this exact problem. A contract-level `rewardPerTokenStored` value increases every time ETH fee revenue is deposited into the contract, scaled by `totalStaked` at that moment. Each address gets a `userRewardPerTokenPaid` checkpoint recorded the last time its position changed. The pending reward for any address is `stakedBalance[addr] * (rewardPerTokenStored - userRewardPerTokenPaid[addr])`, which gets folded into `rewardBalance[addr]` whenever `stake`, `withdraw`, or `claimRewards` runs for that address -- this is what makes rewards accrue continuously and proportionally without the contract needing to loop over every staker.

The three external functions are specified at the signature level only: `stake(uint256 amount)`, `withdraw(uint256 amount)`, and `claimRewards()`. `stake` and `withdraw` move $EMBER principal in and out via the token's own `transferFrom`/`transfer`; `claimRewards` pays out whatever has accumulated in `rewardBalance[msg.sender]` in ETH. The project's dependency set already includes OpenZeppelin's `IERC20` interface (for talking to the deployed $EMBER token) and its `ReentrancyGuard` module, since any function that makes an external call -- a token transfer, an ETH payout -- is a candidate for that protection. Which specific functions actually get the `nonReentrant` modifier, and the exact statement ordering inside each function body, is a per-function decision made as each one is implemented, not settled wholesale here.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Designed EmberStake.sol's storage shape: stakedBalance and rewardBalance mappings keyed by address, a totalStaked counter, and a Synthetix-style rewardPerTokenStored/userRewardPerTokenPaid accumulator so ETH fee revenue distributes proportionally to stake without iterating stakers. stake/withdraw/claimRewards are specified at the signature level only; no function bodies exist yet.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We've locked down exactly what the staking contract needs to remember about each user and how reward sharing will work mathematically, before any of the real code gets written. This removes the risk of redesigning the contract's data after it's already live, which would be expensive to change.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've designed the blueprint for how EmberStake will track who's staked what and how everyone's share of protocol earnings gets calculated fairly. No code has shipped yet -- this is the architecture work that has to happen correctly before building starts, so we don't have to redo it later.

lessons.title: Planning the Test and Audit Process
lessons.summary: Planning a two-tier verification process for EmberStake -- a Hardhat unit test suite covering normal usage, plus a dedicated internal security audit milestone before mainnet with Slither static analysis and an adversarial testing pass -- and stating plainly that the contract has to survive someone actively trying to break it, not just normal use.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Naomi Fitzwilliam, Cinder Labs' Security Lead, sits down with Desmond Okoro before any implementation lands to plan how EmberStake actually gets verified -- not just that it compiles and does the right thing when used correctly, but that it holds up against someone trying to misuse it on purpose. This lesson plans two separate tiers of work: a Hardhat test suite that exercises stake, withdraw, and claimRewards under normal usage across multiple users, and a dedicated internal security audit phase scheduled as its own milestone before mainnet deployment, built around static analysis with Slither and a deliberate adversarial testing pass.

No tests get written in this lesson and no audit happens yet -- this is the plan for both, including what each one is and is not responsible for catching, and when the audit milestone sits relative to the implementation work still ahead.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a bank building a new vault. Before it opens, two different things have to happen. First, the regular staff tests that the vault door opens and closes properly, the lock works, and employees can get in and out the way they're supposed to. That's the easy, expected-use check. Second -- and this is a separate job, done later, by different people -- the bank hires someone whose entire task is to try to break into the vault: pick the lock, find a weak hinge, look for any trick that gets them in a way nobody intended.

This lesson is Naomi and Desmond planning both of those checks for EmberStake, before either one happens. The first check is "does it work right when used normally." The second, separate, later check is "can someone break it on purpose." They're writing down the plan for both today, not running either one yet.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The plan separates two kinds of verification that get conflated far too often in smart contract projects: functional correctness under normal usage, and adversarial robustness under deliberate attack. They require different test design, different mindsets, and -- deliberately, in this plan -- different timing.

The first tier is a Hardhat unit test suite, written in TypeScript against Hardhat's standard Mocha/Chai harness, scoped to correctness: does `stake` correctly increase `stakedBalance` and pull the right amount of $EMBER, does `withdraw` correctly return funds and reject withdrawals larger than a user's balance, does `claimRewards` pay out the right ETH amount, and does the reward-accrual math stay correct across multiple users staking and withdrawing at different times. This suite is planned to run in CI on every change and is explicitly scoped to normal, well-behaved usage.

The second tier is a dedicated internal security audit, planned as a separate milestone that happens once the contract is functionally complete and the unit suite above is passing -- not interleaved with day-to-day implementation work. It has two parts: static analysis with Slither, run against the finished contract to catch known vulnerability patterns automatically (unchecked external calls, integer issues, access-control gaps, reentrancy patterns among them), and a manual adversarial testing pass where Naomi's job is specifically to think like an attacker -- writing malicious contracts that interact with EmberStake in ways a normal user interface never would, and trying to find a sequence of calls that extracts more value than it should.

The plan states its goal plainly, because it's the whole point of having a separate audit milestone at all: this contract has to survive someone actively trying to break it, not just normal usage. The unit suite proves the first half of that. It does not, by itself, prove the second -- which is exactly why the adversarial pass is scheduled as its own milestone before mainnet, rather than assumed to be covered by the happy-path tests that get written alongside the implementation.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Planned two separate verification tiers for EmberStake: a Hardhat/Chai unit suite scoped to normal-usage correctness (stake, withdraw, claimRewards, multi-user reward accrual), and a dedicated internal security audit milestone -- Slither static analysis plus a manual adversarial testing pass -- scheduled after implementation and before mainnet. No tests or audit work exist yet; this is the plan and its scope boundaries only.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We've planned two rounds of checking for the staking contract: first, confirming it works correctly for normal users, and second -- as its own separate, later milestone before we go live -- actively trying to break it the way an attacker would. Both are planned now; neither has started.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've put a plan in place requiring EmberStake to pass two different bars before real money touches it: working correctly for everyday users, and surviving a dedicated internal attempt to break it on purpose. That second check is scheduled as its own milestone before mainnet launch, specifically because normal-use testing alone isn't considered sufficient for a contract holding staked funds.

lessons.title: Planning the Indexer, API, and Deployment Pipeline
lessons.summary: Planning Julian Hargrove's Node.js/TypeScript indexer -- listening to EmberStake's Staked, Withdrawn, and RewardsClaimed events and exposing a REST API for the frontend -- alongside the deployment pipeline: a Base Sepolia testnet deploy first, then a mainnet deployment checklist explicitly gated on the security audit passing.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
With EmberStake's contract design settled and the test/audit plan in place, Julian Hargrove plans the piece that turns raw on-chain activity into something a frontend can actually use: a Node.js/TypeScript indexer service that listens for EmberStake's events and a REST API built on top of what it collects. Desmond and Julian plan this alongside the deployment pipeline those events depend on -- deploying EmberStake to the Base Sepolia testnet first, and a mainnet deployment checklist that explicitly will not let a deploy proceed until the security audit from the previous lesson's plan has actually passed.

Nothing gets deployed and no indexer code gets written in this lesson. This is Julian's architecture plan for the service and Desmond's plan for how and when EmberStake actually goes live on each network.
lessons.explainSimple:
Think of EmberStake as a storefront that rings a bell every time something happens -- someone stakes money, someone takes money out, someone collects their earnings. Julian is planning a listener who sits near that bell all day, writes down every time it rings and what happened, and keeps a notebook other people can look up answers in -- like "how much does this person currently have staked?" -- without them having to go ask the storefront directly every time.

At the same time, Desmond is planning how the storefront itself opens. First it opens in a practice town, where mistakes are cheap and nothing real is at risk. It only gets to open in the real town -- where real money is on the line -- after a very specific inspection has signed off on it first. This lesson is planning both of those things, not doing either yet.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Julian's indexer is planned as an event-driven service subscribed to EmberStake via an RPC provider, using a library such as ethers.js or viem to listen for three specific emitted events: `Staked`, `Withdrawn`, and `RewardsClaimed`. Each event handler is planned to persist what it sees -- staker address, amount, and block/transaction metadata -- into a database the service owns, rather than the frontend ever querying the chain directly for historical activity. The plan explicitly accounts for chain reorganizations: the indexer tracks confirmations and is designed to tolerate a shallow reorg without double-counting an event, rather than treating every emitted log as immediately final.

On top of that stored state, the service exposes a REST API -- planned endpoints include a per-address staking summary and protocol-wide totals -- that the frontend calls instead of hitting an RPC node on every page load. This is a standard separation for any production dApp: the chain is the source of truth, the indexer is a fast, queryable cache of that truth.

The deployment plan runs in two stages. First, EmberStake deploys to Base Sepolia, Base's public testnet, via a Hardhat deploy script, so the full stack -- contract, indexer, API, frontend -- can be exercised end-to-end against a real (if valueless) chain before anything touches mainnet. Second, a mainnet deployment checklist gates the production deploy to Base explicitly on the security audit's completion and sign-off, alongside the usual production-readiness items: verified contract source on the block explorer, a deliberate decision about who holds any privileged/owner role on the deployed contract, and confirmation that the indexer and monitoring are already running against testnet before the same stack points at mainnet. The order is deliberate -- testnet first, audit gate before mainnet, monitoring live before cutover -- and none of it happens until the implementation lessons ahead produce a complete, tested contract to deploy.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Planned Julian's indexer as a standalone Node/TypeScript service subscribed to EmberStake's Staked/Withdrawn/RewardsClaimed events via ethers.js, persisting confirmed events and exposing a REST API (per-address balances, protocol stats, activity history) instead of the frontend hitting RPC directly. Deployment plan: Base Sepolia first, then a mainnet checklist explicitly gated on the security audit passing, verified contract source, and admin-role/monitoring decisions.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We've planned how the frontend will actually get real-time staking data (a backend service watching the contract and serving an API), and we've locked in the deployment order: test network first, and a mainnet launch checklist that cannot be completed until the security audit has passed. Nothing is built or deployed yet.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've planned the backend service that will power the staking dashboard, and -- importantly -- we've set a hard rule that EmberStake cannot go live with real money until the dedicated security audit has passed, on top of a full testnet rehearsal first. This is the launch-readiness plan, not the launch itself.

lessons.title: Writing the $EMBER Token Integration and Staking Logic
lessons.summary: The first real implementation lesson -- writing the actual stake(uint256 amount) and withdraw(uint256 amount) functions in EmberStake.sol, integrating with the already-deployed $EMBER ERC-20 token via IERC20's transferFrom and transfer, and updating the stakedBalance mapping correctly. claimRewards and the reward-accounting logic are deliberately not written here.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Every planning lesson so far has pointed at this moment: Desmond Okoro opens `EmberStake.sol` and writes the first real, working Solidity. This lesson implements exactly two functions -- `stake(uint256 amount)` and `withdraw(uint256 amount)` -- wiring them to the already-deployed $EMBER token via OpenZeppelin's `IERC20` interface, pulling tokens in with `transferFrom` on stake and sending them back out with `transfer` on withdraw, and keeping the `stakedBalance` mapping and `totalStaked` counter correct at every step.

This lesson is scoped to principal handling only. `claimRewards()`, the `rewardPerTokenStored` accumulator, and any ETH payout logic are not written here -- those depend on fee revenue bookkeeping that the design lesson scoped to a separate implementation pass. By the end of this lesson, a user can stake $EMBER into EmberStake and withdraw it back out; earning and claiming rewards still isn't possible yet.
lessons.explainSimple: Think of a coat check at a theater. You hand over your coat (your $EMBER) and the attendant writes your name down on a list with how many coats are yours. Later, you come back, show you're on the list, and get your coat back. That's it -- no tip jar, no rewards, nothing fancy. This lesson is Desmond building exactly that coat check: a real, working way to hand tokens in and get them back out, correctly, every time. The tip-jar rewards system that pays people for leaving their coat there a while gets built separately, next.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Both functions follow the checks-effects-interactions pattern cleanly, because neither one has any reason not to: validate the request, update the contract's own state, and only then make the external call to the token contract. `stake` checks that `amount` is greater than zero, then updates `stakedBalance[msg.sender]` and `totalStaked` before calling `emberToken.transferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), amount)` -- the external call happens last, after the contract's books already reflect the new stake. `withdraw` checks that the caller's `stakedBalance` actually covers the requested `amount`, decrements `stakedBalance[msg.sender]` and `totalStaked` first, and only then calls `emberToken.transfer(msg.sender, amount)` to send the tokens back.

This ordering is the correct, boring choice for these two specific functions: the contract's state is fully consistent before it ever hands control to another contract (the $EMBER token), so there's nothing for an external call to re-enter into that would find stale or exploitable state. That property is a consequence of what `stake` and `withdraw` actually do, not a guarantee that extends automatically to every function EmberStake will eventually have -- which is exactly why the design lesson left the reward-accumulator math and `claimRewards`'s own implementation, including its own external ETH transfer, to a dedicated lesson of its own rather than assuming the same reasoning carries over unexamined.

Both functions emit the events the indexer plan already depends on -- `Staked` and `Withdrawn` -- so Julian's listener has something real to subscribe to once this deploys to Base Sepolia. The $EMBER side of this integration requires the caller to have already called `approve` on the $EMBER token contract for at least `amount`, which `transferFrom` enforces; `stake` is not responsible for granting that allowance itself, and reverts cleanly via the token's own revert if it's missing.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Implemented EmberStake.sol's stake(uint256) and withdraw(uint256): IERC20 transferFrom/transfer against the deployed $EMBER token, stakedBalance and totalStaked updated before the external call in both functions, Staked/Withdrawn events emitted for the indexer. claimRewards() and all reward-accounting logic are explicitly not implemented yet -- next lesson's scope.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: The first real piece of the staking contract is written and working: users can now deposit and withdraw their $EMBER tokens. The rewards piece -- actually earning and claiming ETH for staking -- is a separate implementation step coming next; it isn't live yet.
workplaceExplanation.executive: The core deposit-and-withdraw mechanism for EmberStake is now real, working code -- users will be able to lock up and retrieve their $EMBER tokens. The rewards payout feature is being built next as its own step before this goes any further toward launch.

lessons.title: Writing the Rewards Accounting and claimRewards Function
lessons.summary: Desmond Okoro adds reward accounting to EmberStake.sol -- a distributeRewards() function that credits ETH to stakers proportionally, and a claimRewards() function that lets a staker pull their balance out -- and the team signs off on both as complete and working.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
stake() and withdraw() are already written and working -- EmberStake.sol can take a user's $EMBER in and hand it back out. What it can't do yet is the entire other half of the protocol's value proposition: pay anyone anything. This lesson gives Desmond Okoro, Cinder Labs' smart contract engineer, the two pieces that close that gap.

The first piece is **distributeRewards()** -- the function that gets the ETH collected elsewhere in the Cinder Labs stack (trading fees, withdrawal fees, and other protocol revenue, converted to ETH and forwarded on a schedule) into individual stakers' hands. It's called by a trusted, authorized fee-collector address, and it credits each staker's running reward balance in proportion to how much $EMBER they have staked, relative to everyone else.

The second piece is **claimRewards()** -- the function an EmberStake user actually calls from their own wallet to pull their accumulated ETH rewards out of the contract. Desmond writes it the way a competent engineer writes a withdrawal function on a tight sprint: look up what the caller is owed, send it to them, then clear their balance now that it's been paid. It reads cleanly, it does exactly what the function name says, and by the end of this lesson both functions are live in EmberStake.sol and Vivian Castellan is satisfied the rewards side of the protocol is functionally complete.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a tip jar that a few different coffee shops all pour into at the end of the day, and one trusted person -- the fee collector -- carries that pooled money over to EmberStake and hands it in, saying 'here's today's total, split it up based on how much each person has staked.' The contract does that math and writes down next to each person's name how much they're now owed. That's distributeRewards().

claimRewards() is the other half: it's the counter where a staker walks up and says 'I'd like what you're holding for me.' The contract checks the ledger, hands over exactly that amount of ETH, and then erases the entry -- because once it's been paid out, it shouldn't still say they're owed anything. Desmond writes it in the most natural order a person would think to write it in: look up the amount, hand it over, then cross it off the list.
lessons.explainProfessional:
distributeRewards() is a straightforward proportional-split function: it takes the ETH sent in by the fee collector (`msg.value`) and an array of staker addresses to credit, and for each one computes `(msg.value * stakedBalance[staker]) / totalStaked`, adding that share to a running `rewardBalance[staker]` mapping. It's access-controlled with a dedicated `onlyFeeCollector` modifier rather than reusing `onlyOwner`, since the address calling it day-to-day (an off-chain job Julian Hargrove will eventually wire up) is operationally distinct from the contract owner. The staker list is passed in by the caller rather than iterated on-chain from storage, which keeps gas costs predictable and bounded regardless of how many addresses have ever staked.

claimRewards() is the function a staker calls directly. It reads the caller's accumulated balance out of `rewardBalance`, requires it be greater than zero, sends it as a raw ETH transfer using `.call{value: amount}("")` so the function works even if the recipient is a contract with nontrivial receive logic, requires that call succeed, zeroes out the caller's `rewardBalance` entry, and emits a `RewardsClaimed` event for anything downstream listening to the chain. It's a clean, minimal implementation -- one state read, one external transfer, one state write, one event -- and it's the natural, idiomatic way most engineers reach for a withdrawal pattern on a first pass: check the amount, pay it, record that it's paid. The team reviews both functions against the acceptance criteria from the architecture lesson, confirms the math checks out against a few worked examples by hand, and signs off.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Added distributeRewards() (onlyFeeCollector, splits msg.value proportionally to stakedBalance/totalStaked across a caller-supplied staker list) and claimRewards() (reads rewardBalance[msg.sender], sends ETH via a raw call, zeroes the balance, emits RewardsClaimed) to EmberStake.sol. Verified proportional split and clean claims against a local Hardhat node with two test accounts.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: The rewards side of EmberStake is now functionally complete -- the contract can both receive protocol fee revenue and pay it out to stakers proportionally. Next step is building out full automated test coverage before we consider this locked in.
workplaceExplanation.executive: EmberStake can now actually pay stakers their share of protocol revenue in ETH, not just hold their staked tokens. That's the core value proposition of the product now working end to end in our development environment.

lessons.title: Writing the Hardhat Test Suite
lessons.summary: Desmond Okoro writes a Hardhat/TypeScript test suite covering staking, withdrawing, reward distribution, and claiming rewards for normal wallet accounts -- every test passes, and the team feels good about coverage going into the testnet deployment.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
EmberStake.sol now has stake(), withdraw(), distributeRewards(), and claimRewards() all written -- but 'written' and 'tested' are two different things, and nothing has actually verified any of it beyond Desmond's one manual sanity check in the last lesson. This lesson builds the real thing: a Hardhat test suite in TypeScript, using Chai's assertion library and Hardhat's network helpers, that exercises every one of those four functions the way Cinder Labs' actual users will.

Desmond organizes the suite the way most teams organize a contract's first real test pass: by feature. A `describe` block for staking, one for withdrawing, one for reward distribution, and one for claiming -- each with the normal, expected scenarios (stake succeeds and updates balances, withdraw succeeds and returns tokens, a fair distribution lands the right amount in each staker's reward balance, a staker with a balance can claim it and the balance zeroes out afterward) plus the obvious guard-rail cases (staking zero, claiming with nothing to claim, a non-fee-collector address trying to call distributeRewards). Every test runs against ordinary wallet accounts from Hardhat's local signer list -- the same kind of address any real EmberStake user would connect with.

By the end of the lesson, `npx hardhat test` runs green across the board, Desmond pulls a coverage report, and the team -- genuinely, not performatively -- feels confident shipping this to a testnet. Nothing in this lesson suggests there's anything left uncovered.
lessons.explainSimple:
Think about a bike manufacturer that, before shipping a new bike model, has a few different ordinary riders take it for a spin -- uphill, downhill, braking hard, carrying groceries -- and checks that everything works the way it's supposed to every time. That's what this lesson does for EmberStake: it has a bunch of 'ordinary rider' tests, each one checking that a normal person using the contract the normal way gets exactly the result they should.

Desmond writes a test for staking tokens, a test for taking them back out, a test for the reward money getting split up fairly, and a test for an ordinary person claiming their share and it landing in their wallet correctly. He runs all of them, and they all pass -- green across the board. That's a real, honest green light: every one of those ordinary-use situations works exactly as intended, and the team is right to feel good about it.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The suite is structured around a shared `deployFixture()` using `loadFixture` from `@nomicfoundation/hardhat-network-helpers`, which deploys a fresh EmberStake instance (plus a mock ERC-20 `EmberToken`), mints and approves $EMBER for a handful of named signers, and sets the fee-collector role -- keeping every test isolated from shared mutable state. From there, `describe` blocks cover staking (balance and `totalStaked` updates, zero-amount revert), withdrawing (balance and `totalStaked` decrease, over-withdraw revert), reward distribution (proportional crediting across multiple stakers verified with exact arithmetic, non-fee-collector-caller revert), and claiming (a staker's ETH balance increases by exactly their `rewardBalance`, that balance reads back as zero afterward, and a zero-balance claim reverts with the expected message).

Every claim-path test exercises a normal externally-owned account as the claimer -- a Hardhat signer backed by a plain private key, with no contract code at its address and no custom logic running on receipt of ETH. That's a deliberate, reasonable choice for a first test pass: it's the overwhelmingly common case (nearly every EmberStake user is a regular wallet, not a smart contract), it's the fastest and simplest scenario to write and assert against, and it's exactly the kind of coverage a team writes before a testnet deployment to validate the happy path end to end. The suite runs via `npx hardhat test`, all green, and a `solidity-coverage` run shows every line of the four core functions exercised. The team reviews the report together and signs off on it as solid coverage heading into deployment.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Wrote a Chai/Hardhat test suite using loadFixture for isolated state, covering stake/withdraw balance updates, proportional reward distribution math, and reward claims for normal EOA signers, plus the standard revert cases (zero stake, unauthorized distributeRewards caller, zero-balance claim). All 9 tests pass; solidity-coverage shows full line coverage on the four core functions.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We now have a full automated test suite covering every core function of the staking contract -- staking, withdrawing, reward distribution, and claiming. Everything passes, and the team reviewed the coverage report together before agreeing we're ready to move toward testnet.
workplaceExplanation.executive: The staking and rewards contract has now been automatically tested against every normal way our users will interact with it, and it passed every check. That gives us real confidence as we move toward putting this live on a public test network.

lessons.title: Building the Indexer and REST API
lessons.summary: Julian Hargrove builds a Node.js/TypeScript indexer that listens for Staked, Withdrawn, and RewardsClaimed events from EmberStake.sol, stores them, and exposes a REST API the frontend will use for total staked, a user's stake, and their claimable rewards.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
EmberStake.sol is written and tested, but right now the only way to know what's happening inside it is to query the chain directly, call by call -- which is exactly how you don't build a usable product frontend. This lesson gives Julian Hargrove, Cinder Labs' backend/infrastructure engineer, the service that sits between the contract and everything that needs to display its data quickly: an **indexer** that listens for every `Staked`, `Withdrawn`, and `RewardsClaimed` event the contract emits, stores them, and a **REST API** on top that answers the questions the frontend will actually ask.

The indexer is a Node.js/TypeScript service using `ethers.js` to subscribe to EmberStake's event logs in real time and to backfill any history it missed while it was offline, writing each event into a local database as a durable, queryable record. The API that reads from that database is a small Express app with three endpoints that matter for launch: total ETH and $EMBER currently staked across the protocol, a specific user's current stake, and that user's current claimable reward balance (read live from the contract itself, since it can change between indexed events). Julian builds this cleanly and correctly -- there's no bug to find here, just a real, working piece of infrastructure the frontend team will build on top of starting next.
lessons.explainSimple:
Picture a busy train station with one single announcer who has to personally walk up to every single train, ask the conductor where it's going, and then relay that to anyone who asks -- for every question, every time. That's what talking directly to the blockchain for every page load would be like: slow, and it doesn't scale.

Julian builds something much better: a station departures board. A dedicated worker (the indexer) stands near the tracks all day, watches every train come and go, and writes it down the instant it happens. Anyone who wants to know what's going on -- how many people are staked right now, what one specific person has staked, what they're owed -- just glances at the board (the API) instead of running down to the platform themselves. The board stays accurate, and anyone can check it instantly.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The indexer runs as a standalone Node.js/TypeScript process using `ethers.js`'s `Contract` interface to both backfill historical logs via `queryFilter` across a bounded block range on startup, and subscribe live via `contract.on(...)` for `Staked`, `Withdrawn`, and `RewardsClaimed` going forward. Each event is written to a local SQLite database (via `better-sqlite3`) as an append-only `events` table keyed by transaction hash and log index, which makes the indexer safely restartable -- re-processing an already-seen event is a no-op rather than a duplicate write.

The REST API is a thin Express layer reading from that same database, plus one live contract read where staleness would actually matter. `GET /stats` aggregates the `events` table for protocol-wide totals (current total staked, derived from summing `Staked` and `Withdrawn` amounts). `GET /users/:address/stake` returns that address's current staked balance, computed the same way from its event history. `GET /users/:address/rewards` is the one endpoint that calls the contract directly rather than the local database -- `emberStake.rewardBalance(address)` -- because a user's claimable balance can change between indexed events (a fresh `distributeRewards()` batch) and the frontend needs the true current figure, not a slightly stale derived one. Julian unit-tests the indexer's event-to-database mapping against a local Hardhat node emitting real events, confirms the API's numbers match a manual on-chain check, and the team signs off on it as ready for the frontend to build against.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Built a Node.js/TypeScript indexer (ethers.js, better-sqlite3) that backfills and live-subscribes to Staked/Withdrawn/RewardsClaimed events into an append-only events table, plus an Express REST API exposing /stats, /users/:address/stake (derived from indexed events), and /users/:address/rewards (a live contract read, since claimable balances change between indexed events). Verified against a local Hardhat node.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We now have a service that tracks everything happening on the staking contract and exposes it through a simple API the frontend can build against -- total staked, a user's stake, and what they can claim. This unblocks the frontend team starting now.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've built the piece of infrastructure that lets our app show users real-time information about their staking position and rewards, without the app having to talk to the blockchain directly every time someone loads a page.

lessons.title: Deploying to Base Sepolia Testnet
lessons.summary: Desmond Okoro deploys EmberStake.sol to Base Sepolia via a Hardhat deployment script, verifies the contract on Basescan, and Julian Hargrove points the indexer and API at the live testnet deployment.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Everything so far -- the contract, the tests, the indexer, the API -- has only ever run against a local Hardhat node that resets the moment the process stops. This lesson moves EmberStake off of Desmond's laptop and onto **Base Sepolia**, the public testnet for Base, so the rest of Cinder Labs -- the frontend team, Vivian for demos, eventually Naomi for a security review -- can interact with a real, persistent, publicly inspectable deployment.

Desmond writes a Hardhat deployment script that deploys `EmberStake.sol` to Base Sepolia, records the deployed address, and then verifies the contract's source code on **Basescan** (Base's block explorer) so anyone can read the exact Solidity that's actually running at that address -- not just trust a label. Once the contract is live and verified, Julian updates the indexer and API from the last lesson to point at the real Base Sepolia RPC endpoint and the real deployed contract address instead of a local Hardhat node, and confirms the whole stack -- contract, indexer, API -- works identically against the live testnet as it did locally. The team runs through a full stake-distribute-claim cycle on Base Sepolia together, it all behaves exactly as expected, and everyone is satisfied EmberStake is ready for the next phase of testing.
lessons.explainSimple:
Think of this like moving a lemonade stand from your own driveway, where only your family ever sees it, out to the fairgrounds, where it still isn't the real, final farmers' market but it's a real public spot other people can actually walk up to and try. Base Sepolia is that fairgrounds -- a real, shared, public place to test things, just with play money instead of real money.

Desmond sets the stand up out there (deploys the contract), puts a sign next to it listing the exact recipe so nobody has to just take his word for it (verifying the source code on the block explorer), and then Julian makes sure the order board (the indexer and API) is actually watching the real stand at the fairgrounds instead of still watching the one back in the driveway. The team buys a lemonade, pays, and gets a receipt -- a full real test, right there in public, and it works.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The deployment script uses Hardhat's standard deployment pattern, targeting a `baseSepolia` network entry in `hardhat.config.ts` configured with Base Sepolia's public RPC URL and a deployer private key loaded from the environment. The script deploys `EmberStake`, waits for the deployment transaction to be mined, and writes the resulting contract address and deployment block number to a small JSON artifact that both the verification step and the indexer's `.env` will read from -- the indexer needs that deployment block as its backfill starting point rather than scanning from block zero.

Contract verification runs via Hardhat's Etherscan-compatible verify plugin, configured with Base Sepolia's verification API endpoint, which uploads the exact source and compiler settings so Basescan can confirm the deployed bytecode matches and display the readable Solidity source directly on the contract's page -- the standard way anyone, including an eventual external auditor, independently confirms what code is actually running rather than trusting a description of it. Once verified, Julian updates the indexer's `RPC_URL`, `CONTRACT_ADDRESS`, and `DEPLOY_BLOCK` environment variables to point at the live Base Sepolia deployment, restarts the service, and confirms it backfills cleanly from the real deployment block with zero gaps. The team then runs one full real cycle end to end on the public testnet -- stake, a simulated fee-collector distribution, a claim -- and every number the API reports matches what Basescan shows for the same transactions, which is exactly the cross-check that matters before calling a testnet deployment done.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Deployed EmberStake to Base Sepolia (chainId 84532) via a Hardhat deployment script, verified the contract source on Basescan through the Etherscan-compatible verify plugin, and repointed the indexer/API's RPC_URL, CONTRACT_ADDRESS, and DEPLOY_BLOCK at the live deployment. Ran a full stake/distribute/claim cycle on the public testnet and cross-checked every number against Basescan.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: EmberStake is now live on a public test network, not just running locally, and the indexer and API are both pointed at the real deployment. We ran a complete test cycle together today -- staking, reward distribution, and a claim -- and everything worked exactly as expected.
workplaceExplanation.executive: Our staking contract is now live on a public test environment where the whole team, and eventually outside reviewers, can interact with the real thing. We tested a full cycle end to end today and it worked cleanly.

lessons.title: A Full Testnet Staking Cycle: Dress Rehearsal
lessons.summary: With EmberStake.sol live on Base Sepolia, Desmond Okoro and Julian Hargrove run a full end-to-end rehearsal with real test wallets -- stake, accrue fees, distribute rewards, claim, withdraw -- and every normal-wallet flow comes back clean.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
EmberStake.sol has been deployed to Base Sepolia for a few days now, and Julian Hargrove's indexer/API has been quietly logging every on-chain event against it. Before anyone starts talking seriously about mainnet, Desmond Okoro wants to see the whole lifecycle happen for real, end to end, with real test wallets doing real transactions -- not another Hardhat unit test asserting a balance in isolation.

This lesson is that rehearsal. Desmond funds five test wallets with Base Sepolia ETH and testnet $EMBER from the faucet the team set up earlier, then walks each one through the full cycle by hand: `stake()` into EmberStake.sol, wait through a few blocks while protocol fees accrue and rewards accumulate into each wallet's `rewardBalance`, call `claimRewards()` to pull out the ETH reward, and for a couple of wallets, call `withdraw()` to pull the staked $EMBER back out too. Julian watches the indexer the whole time, confirming every `Staked`, `RewardsClaimed`, and `Withdrawn` event lands in the API exactly the way the frontend will eventually expect it.

Everything works. Stakes register correctly, rewards calculate and distribute the way the reward-accrual logic was designed to, `claimRewards()` sends the right ETH amount to the right wallet every time, and `withdraw()` returns principal cleanly with no stuck funds anywhere. Vivian Castellan sits in for the second half of the run and signs off that the core user journey -- the thing a real $EMBER holder will actually do -- works exactly as promised. Every wallet in this rehearsal is an ordinary externally-owned account, the same kind any real user would connect with MetaMask or Coinbase Wallet. Nobody in this lesson tries to stake, claim, or withdraw from a smart contract instead of a normal wallet, because nobody's thought to ask that question yet -- the test suite and this rehearsal both exercise the same category of user, and both come back green.
lessons.explainSimple:
Before a restaurant opens its doors to real customers, the staff runs a full dinner service with no paying guests -- they cook every dish on the menu, carry it to a table, let a coworker "order," "eat," and "pay," start to finish, just to prove the whole night actually works when it's strung together instead of tested one station at a time.

Desmond and Julian do the same thing with EmberStake. They hand a handful of test wallets some pretend tokens, then walk each one through the entire experience a real user would have: lock up tokens to start earning, wait while rewards build up, cash out the reward, and pull the original tokens back out. Every single step works exactly the way it's supposed to, and Julian's tracking system records every move correctly.

There's one thing worth noticing, even though nobody in the room notices it yet: every single test wallet in this rehearsal is just an ordinary wallet, like a regular customer walking in the front door. Nobody tries anything unusual or adversarial. That's a completely reasonable rehearsal to run -- it's just not the same thing as asking "what if someone walks in and tries to cheat?"
lessons.explainProfessional:
This rehearsal validates something a Hardhat unit test, by design, usually doesn't: behavioral correctness of the full lifecycle under real block timing, against a real deployed instance, observed through the same indexing layer the production frontend will eventually read from. Confirming that `Staked`, `RewardsClaimed`, and `Withdrawn` events land in Julian's API exactly as emitted, in the right order, with the right payloads, closes a different gap than unit coverage of `claimRewards()`'s arithmetic ever could.

It's worth being precise about what this lesson does and doesn't prove, because the distinction matters a great deal very soon. Every wallet exercising the contract here is an externally-owned account (EOA) -- a private-key-controlled wallet with no code of its own, incapable of executing logic when it receives ETH. `claimRewards()`'s external call via `msg.sender.call{value: amount}("")` sends ETH to each of these wallets, and an EOA simply has no `receive()` or fallback function to run in response; the call just deposits ETH and returns. That's the entire reason this rehearsal, run faithfully and thoroughly, can pass every single check without ever touching the one condition that matters for a reentrancy vulnerability.

A reentrancy attack is not a bug that shows up under normal-wallet load, no matter how many cycles you run or how real the test wallets are -- it requires the caller itself to be a smart contract with code in its `receive()` function that re-enters the vulnerable function before state is finalized. Nothing about this rehearsal was designed to probe that, and nothing about it should have been: it's a legitimate, necessary dress rehearsal of the happy path, not a security audit, and the two are different disciplines run by design at different points in the plan. The gap this lesson leaves open is exact and specific, and it's the gap the team's dedicated audit, still ahead of them, exists to close.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Fund five real test wallets

Desmond funds five fresh wallets on Base Sepolia using the project's existing faucet script, giving each one testnet ETH for gas and testnet $EMBER to stake:

```bash
npx hardhat run scripts/fund-testnet-wallets.js --network baseSepolia
```

```
Funded 5 wallets on Base Sepolia:
  0xA11c... 2.0 ETH, 5,000 EMBER
  0xB22d... 2.0 ETH, 12,000 EMBER
  0xC33e... 2.0 ETH, 3,500 EMBER
  0xD44f... 2.0 ETH, 8,000 EMBER
  0xE55a... 2.0 ETH, 20,000 EMBER
```

All five are ordinary externally-owned accounts (EOAs) -- the same kind of wallet any real $EMBER holder would connect to the dApp.

## Step 2 -- Stake from each wallet

Each wallet calls `stake()` on EmberStake.sol with a different amount, to exercise a realistic spread of position sizes:

```javascript
const tx = await emberStake.connect(walletA).stake(ethers.parseEther("5000"));
await tx.wait();
// Staked(0xA11c..., 5000000000000000000000) emitted
```

Julian confirms each `Staked` event lands correctly in the indexer's `/positions` endpoint within a block or two of confirmation.

## Step 3 -- Let rewards accrue across real blocks

Desmond lets several real blocks pass on Base Sepolia -- not a Hardhat `evm_increaseTime` shortcut -- so the reward-accrual logic runs against genuine block timestamps the way it will on mainnet. The team checks `rewardBalance` for each wallet directly:

```javascript
await emberStake.rewardBalance(walletA.address);
// 0.0412 ETH
```

Values track proportionally with stake size, exactly as the reward-rate design intended.

## Step 4 -- Claim rewards

Each wallet calls `claimRewards()` and the team confirms the ETH actually lands in the wallet and `rewardBalance` zeroes out afterward:

```javascript
const before = await ethers.provider.getBalance(walletA.address);
await emberStake.connect(walletA).claimRewards();
const after = await ethers.provider.getBalance(walletA.address);
// after - before ~= 0.0412 ETH (minus gas)
```

```
RewardsClaimed(0xA11c..., 41200000000000000) -- indexed correctly
```

Five for five, correct amount, correct wallet, every time.

## Step 5 -- Withdraw stake on a couple of wallets

Two of the five wallets also call `withdraw()` to pull their original $EMBER back out, confirming principal returns cleanly with no rounding loss or stuck balance:

```javascript
await emberStake.connect(walletC).withdraw(ethers.parseEther("3500"));
// Withdrawn(0xC33e..., 3500000000000000000000) -- EMBER balance restored
```

## Step 6 -- Vivian signs off on the happy path

```
TESTNET REHEARSAL SIGN-OFF -- EmberStake.sol, Base Sepolia
  Stake (5 wallets):          PASS, all events indexed correctly
  Reward accrual (real blocks): PASS, proportional to stake size
  claimRewards (5 wallets):    PASS, correct ETH amount every time
  withdraw (2 wallets):        PASS, principal returned cleanly
  Indexer/API consistency:     PASS, matches on-chain state
  Sign-off: Vivian Castellan -- "the real user journey works."
```

Every wallet used in this rehearsal is a normal, private-key-controlled account. Nobody connects a smart contract to the protocol and tries to claim through it -- that question hasn't come up yet.

## Step 7 -- Cross-check against Julian's indexer one more time

Before closing out, Desmond pulls the indexer's own summary view for all five wallets and diffs it against the raw on-chain state one more time, just to be thorough:

```
GET /positions/summary
[
  { "wallet": "0xA11c...", "staked": "1500", "claimed": "0.0412" },
  { "wallet": "0xB22d...", "staked": "12000", "claimed": "0.0989" },
  { "wallet": "0xC33e...", "staked": "0", "claimed": "0.0287" },
  { "wallet": "0xD44f...", "staked": "8000", "claimed": "0.0661" },
  { "wallet": "0xE55a...", "staked": "20000", "claimed": "0.1654" }
]
```

Every figure matches the on-chain reads exactly. Julian closes the ticket he'd opened to track this rehearsal, and Desmond writes a short note in the project log confirming the full lifecycle -- stake, accrue, claim, withdraw -- is production-correct for the kind of wallet a real user actually is.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Ran a full end-to-end rehearsal of EmberStake.sol on Base Sepolia with five funded test wallets: stake, reward accrual over real blocks, claimRewards, and withdraw all passed cleanly, and Julian confirmed every Staked/RewardsClaimed/Withdrawn event indexed correctly. All five wallets were standard EOAs -- no contract-based or adversarial callers were exercised in this pass.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We ran a full real-world rehearsal of the staking flow on the test network today -- staking, earning rewards, claiming them, and withdrawing -- using real test wallets end to end, and everything worked exactly as designed. Vivian signed off on the core user journey.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We put the staking feature through a complete dry run on our test network this week, simulating the exact journey a real token holder will take, and it performed flawlessly. We're on track for the final pre-launch review.

lessons.title: Preparing for Mainnet: The Final Checklist and the Audit Kickoff
lessons.summary: Desmond Okoro and Julian Hargrove work through a mainnet-readiness checklist -- gas optimization, access-control review, final documentation -- and Vivian Castellan formally kicks off Naomi Fitzwilliam's dedicated internal security audit as the last gate before deploying to Base mainnet.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
The testnet rehearsal went smoothly, but Vivian Castellan isn't willing to schedule a mainnet deployment date off the strength of a happy-path dry run alone -- EmberStake.sol will hold real $EMBER and real ETH the moment it goes live on Base mainnet, and a mistake there isn't recoverable the way a testnet mistake is. This lesson is the last stretch of preparation before anyone touches mainnet, and it ends with the one gate the team agreed all the way back when they first scoped this project: a dedicated internal security audit, run by someone whose only job in this project is to try to break it.

Desmond and Julian work through a mainnet-readiness checklist together. Desmond reviews EmberStake.sol for gas optimization -- tightening storage reads, checking for unnecessary SLOAD operations in `claimRewards()` and `withdraw()`, confirming the contract won't be needlessly expensive for real users paying real gas on mainnet. He also reviews access control line by line: which functions are `external`, which are gated by `onlyOwner` or a role modifier, and whether any state-changing function is reachable by an address it shouldn't be. Julian finishes the final documentation pass -- deployment runbook, indexer API reference, and a one-page incident-response contact list -- so nothing about running this in production depends on tribal knowledge sitting only in Desmond's head.

With that checklist clean, Vivian formally kicks off the audit the team planned back when they first scoped this project: Naomi Fitzwilliam, Cinder Labs' Security Lead, steps in as a dedicated, adversarial reviewer whose explicit job is to try to find a way to break EmberStake.sol before a real attacker does. Vivian sets the scope and the stakes in the kickoff meeting -- nothing ships to mainnet until Naomi signs off -- and Naomi starts her review that same day. This lesson ends right there, at the moment the audit begins. Nothing has been found yet.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a company is about to move into a brand-new office building for the first time. Before anyone unpacks a single box, there's a final walkthrough: make sure the lights aren't wasting electricity, make sure only the right people have keys to the right rooms, and make sure the building manual is written down somewhere instead of living only in one person's memory.

That's what Desmond and Julian do here. Desmond checks that the contract isn't accidentally wasteful with the "gas" fees real users will pay, and double-checks that only the right people and processes can trigger the sensitive actions. Julian makes sure the instructions for running everything are actually written down.

Then comes the big moment: before anyone moves real money in, the company hires an inspector whose entire job is to try to find a way to break into the building -- not to approve it, but to genuinely attempt to find a flaw. That inspector is Naomi. Vivian is the one who officially says "go ahead, start trying to break it," and that's exactly where this lesson ends -- the inspection has just started, and nobody knows yet what she'll find.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A gas-optimization and access-control pass immediately before a security audit is a deliberate sequencing choice, not busywork: it's considerably more efficient for Naomi to audit a contract that's already been cleaned up for the mundane stuff, so her adversarial attention goes toward exploitability rather than toward flagging an unnecessary `SLOAD` the team already knew about. Reviewing `claimRewards()` and `withdraw()` specifically for redundant storage reads is standard practice on a contract expected to see real mainnet transaction volume, where every extra storage operation is a real cost passed directly to the user.

The access-control review matters for a different reason: it's the review pass most likely to catch a class of bug that has nothing to do with arithmetic correctness -- a function that should be `onlyOwner`-gated but isn't, or a role check that's present but checks the wrong condition. Walking every `external` function against its intended caller set, line by line, before the audit starts is what makes the subsequent audit a search for subtler problems rather than a first-pass catch of something this review should have found on its own.

The real significance of this lesson, though, is organizational: Vivian's kickoff formally converts "we planned to do a security audit eventually" into "the audit is the gate, and nothing ships to mainnet until it clears." That's a meaningfully different commitment than an informal code review squeezed in before launch, and naming it as the explicit, non-negotiable last gate -- rather than one more item on the mainnet checklist -- is precisely what gives Naomi's adversarial findings, whatever they turn out to be, the organizational weight to actually delay a launch date if they need to. The checklist closes this lesson clean. The audit itself has not produced a single finding yet, by design -- that's the next lesson.

## Step 1 -- Gas optimization review

Desmond walks through EmberStake.sol's state-changing functions looking for unnecessary storage reads, since every `SLOAD` is a real cost a mainnet user pays in gas:

    require(rewardBalance[msg.sender] > 0, "No rewards to claim");
    uint256 amount = rewardBalance[msg.sender]; // second SLOAD, same slot
    ...
}

// After: read once, reuse the local variable
function claimRewards() external {
    uint256 amount = rewardBalance[msg.sender]; // single SLOAD
    require(amount > 0, "No rewards to claim");
    ...
}
```

He runs a gas report to confirm the cleanup actually moved the number:

```

lessons.title: The Audit Test That Drained the Reward Pool
lessons.summary: Naomi Fitzwilliam's Slither scan flags claimRewards() with a reentrancy-eth warning, and the malicious attacker contract she writes to check it proves she can drain EmberStake's entire ETH reward pool for multiple users in a single transaction on a local Hardhat fork -- confirmed and reported, not yet fixed.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Naomi Fitzwilliam's audit starts the way any serious Solidity audit starts: with static analysis, before a single line of adversarial test code gets written. She runs Slither against EmberStake.sol, and it comes back with a `reentrancy-eth` warning pointed directly at `claimRewards()` -- Slither's detector for exactly this pattern, an external call that sends ETH before the contract updates its own state. The warning on its own isn't proof of anything; Slither flags plenty of patterns that turn out to be harmless in context, and Naomi knows that treating every static-analysis warning as a confirmed vulnerability would make her audit worthless within a week. So she does what distinguishes a real auditor from a linter: she tries to actually exploit it.

She writes a malicious attacker contract from scratch and adds it to the Hardhat test suite -- a `ReentrancyAttacker.sol` with nothing unusual about it except one deliberate detail: its `receive()` function calls `claimRewards()` on EmberStake.sol again, every time it receives ETH. She deploys this attacker on a local Hardhat fork of the actual Base Sepolia deployment -- the real, currently-live contract, forked locally so nothing on the real testnet is touched -- stakes through the attacker contract to build up a reward balance, and then calls `claimRewards()` once.

That single call is enough. Because `claimRewards()` sends the ETH before zeroing `rewardBalance[msg.sender]`, the attacker's `receive()` function fires mid-transfer and calls `claimRewards()` again -- and again, and again, each time before the first call ever gets the chance to zero the balance out. Every one of those nested calls reads the same, still-unzeroed `rewardBalance` and pays out again. Naomi's test proves this isn't limited to draining the attacker's own stake: because the contract's ETH balance is shared across every staker's accrued rewards, the recursive calls keep paying out of that shared pool until it's empty, meaning a single malicious contract, calling `claimRewards()` exactly once from the outside, can drain the ETH owed to every other real staker too -- not just its own. One transaction. The entire reward pool. Naomi confirms the result, writes it up precisely, and reports it to Desmond Okoro and Vivian Castellan immediately. The vulnerability is understood and proven exploitable. Nothing has been fixed yet.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a bank teller who, when you ask to withdraw your savings, hands you the cash first and only afterward updates the paper ledger to say your account is now at zero. Most of the time that's fine -- you take your cash, you leave, the ledger gets updated a second later, nobody notices the gap.

But imagine a customer who, the instant the cash touches their hands, has a trick that lets them instantly ask for another withdrawal before the ledger gets updated -- and the teller, having no updated ledger to check yet, just hands over more cash. And does it again. And again, dozens of times, in the blink of an eye, all before the ledger ever catches up -- not just emptying their own account, but the whole vault, which has everyone's money sitting in it together.

That's exactly the trick Naomi finds. A tool called Slither flags something suspicious about the order of operations in the code first -- like a building inspector flagging a door that locks in the wrong order. Naomi doesn't just trust the flag; she builds a fake "customer" -- a malicious contract -- specifically designed to try that trick for real, on a safe practice copy of the real system. It works. One single request drains the entire shared pool of money, not just the fake customer's own share. She immediately tells Desmond and Vivian exactly what she found. Nobody's fixed it yet -- that happens next.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This lesson is worth reading as a template for how a real audit should work, step by step. Static analysis first: Slither's `reentrancy-eth` detector exists precisely to flag an external call (`.call{value: amount}("")`) that precedes a state write to the same storage slot the call's outcome depends on -- exactly the shape of `claimRewards()`. That's a legitimate, specific signal, not a generic warning. But a signal is not a proof, and Naomi's discipline here is the discipline that separates a useful audit from a wall of unactioned linter noise: she doesn't report the Slither finding as-is, she builds the exploit.

`ReentrancyAttacker.sol`'s `receive()` function calling back into `claimRewards()` is the textbook reentrancy primitive, and running it against a local Hardhat fork of the actual live Base Sepolia deployment -- rather than a freshly redeployed clean copy -- matters more than it might look: forking the real deployment means the exploit is proven against the exact bytecode and exact state that's currently live, closing any gap between "this is theoretically exploitable" and "this specific deployment is exploitable right now."

The mechanism itself is worth stating precisely, because it's the detail later lessons depend on: `claimRewards()` reads `rewardBalance[msg.sender]` into `amount`, sends `amount` in ETH via a low-level `call`, and only then sets `rewardBalance[msg.sender] = 0`. Within that `call`, if `msg.sender` is a contract with a `receive()` that calls `claimRewards()` again, the function executes again with `rewardBalance[msg.sender]` still unchanged -- the checks-effects-interactions pattern is violated in the one specific way that matters: effects (the zeroing) happen after interactions (the external call), not before. And because EmberStake.sol holds one shared ETH balance funding every staker's `rewardBalance` entry, the recursive drain isn't bounded by the attacker's own stake -- it's bounded only by the contract's total ETH balance, meaning the blast radius of this bug is every honest staker's unclaimed rewards, not just the attacker's own. Confirmed, scoped, reported to Desmond and Vivian. The fix -- and it has to be more than a one-line reorder -- is the next lesson.

One external call drained the entire shared ETH reward pool (2.84 ETH across 11 stakers) in a single transaction via 6 nested reentrant calls. Reported to Desmond and Vivian. Not yet fixed.

This is exactly why we built in a dedicated audit before mainnet. She's confirmed it's real and reported it; the fix starts immediately.

A flaw in how the contract pays out rewards could have let someone drain shared funds in a single transaction. No real money was ever at risk; this was caught and proven on our test environment before mainnet. We're fixing it now and it will be independently re-verified before we proceed.

lessons.title: Fixing the Reentrancy and Locking It In With a Permanent Test
lessons.summary: Desmond Okoro fixes claimRewards() by moving the state update before the external call, adds OpenZeppelin's ReentrancyGuard as defense-in-depth, and Naomi Fitzwilliam's malicious-attacker-contract test gets added permanently to the CI suite -- re-run against the fixed contract to confirm the exploit now fails.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Naomi's finding gave Desmond Okoro something precise to fix, and he treats it as three separate, deliberate changes rather than one quick patch -- because a reentrancy bug that just gets patched in the one place it was found is a reentrancy bug that can come back the next time someone touches this contract.

The first and most direct fix is reordering `claimRewards()` so the effect -- zeroing `rewardBalance[msg.sender]` -- happens before the interaction -- the external ETH transfer. That single reordering closes the exact exploit Naomi proved: by the time `ReentrancyAttacker`'s `receive()` fires and tries to call `claimRewards()` again, `rewardBalance[msg.sender]` already reads zero, and the `require(amount > 0, ...)` check on the re-entrant call fails immediately.

The second fix is defense-in-depth, and Desmond adds it deliberately even though the reorder alone would have stopped this specific exploit: he pulls in OpenZeppelin's `ReentrancyGuard` and marks `claimRewards()` `nonReentrant`. The reasoning is straightforward and a little humbling -- the ordering fix stops this bug today, but it relies on every future engineer who touches this function remembering to keep effects before interactions forever. A `nonReentrant` modifier doesn't depend on anyone remembering anything; it makes a second, independent reentrant call into the same function revert outright, so even a future reordering mistake elsewhere in the contract gets caught by the guard instead of shipping.

The third fix is the one Desmond and Naomi both insist on, and it's not a code change to EmberStake.sol at all: Naomi's `ReentrancyAttacker` test doesn't stay a one-off proof-of-concept she ran locally during the audit. It gets added permanently to the Hardhat test suite that runs in CI on every single commit, from here forward. The team re-runs it against the fixed contract first, confirming the exploit that drained the entire pool in lesson 15 now reverts cleanly, and then confirms it stays in the suite going forward -- so if anyone, ever, reintroduces this exact ordering mistake in a future change, the next CI run catches it before it ships, instead of waiting for another dedicated audit to find it by hand.
lessons.explainSimple:
Remember the bank teller who handed over cash before updating the ledger, letting a clever customer ask for more money before the ledger ever caught up? Here's the fix, done three different ways, on purpose.

First, the obvious fix: update the ledger the instant the customer asks to withdraw, before handing over a single dollar. Now if that same trick gets tried again, the ledger already says zero, and the teller refuses.

Second, a backup lock, in case the first fix ever gets undone by accident later: a rule that says nobody can ask this teller for a second withdrawal while their first one is still being processed, full stop, no exceptions, no matter what order anyone writes the steps in. That way, even if a future employee accidentally brings back the old bad habit somewhere else in the building, this second rule still catches it.

Third, and maybe the most important one: the fake-customer trick Naomi invented to prove the problem was real doesn't just get thrown away once the fix works. It becomes a permanent, automatic test that runs every single time anyone changes anything about this system, forever -- so if this exact mistake ever tries to sneak back in, a robot catches it immediately, instead of everyone hoping a human auditor happens to catch it again by luck.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The three fixes map cleanly onto three different failure modes, which is exactly why collapsing them into a single patch would have been a mistake. The ordering fix addresses the specific bug Naomi found: moving `rewardBalance[msg.sender] = 0` before the external `call` restores checks-effects-interactions ordering, so a re-entrant call to `claimRewards()` reads a zeroed balance and fails its own `require(amount > 0, ...)` check before it can do anything. This is the correct, minimal fix for this exact function, and it's necessary -- but treating it as sufficient would be a mistake, because it's a single-point fix that depends entirely on every future change to this contract preserving the same discipline.

That's precisely the gap OpenZeppelin's `ReentrancyGuard` closes. The `nonReentrant` modifier works by setting a status flag to `_ENTERED` on entry and checking it isn't already set, reverting any nested call into a `nonReentrant`-guarded function on the same contract regardless of call ordering inside the function body. It's redundant with the ordering fix today, by design -- and that redundancy is the entire point. If a future engineer, months from now, adds a new reward-adjustment path that accidentally reintroduces an external call before a state write, the ordering discipline alone offers no protection; the guard still does, because it doesn't care what order the function's internals are written in. Defense-in-depth here isn't decorative -- it's the difference between a fix that depends on institutional memory and one that doesn't.

The third fix is the one most teams skip under launch pressure, and it's arguably the one that matters most over the contract's lifetime: Naomi's exploit test moves from a local, one-off proof-of-concept into the permanent CI suite, re-run on every commit from here forward. Re-running it first against the fixed contract and confirming it now reverts is the validation step that closes this incident -- proof the fix works, not just confidence that it should. Keeping it in CI permanently is what prevents this exact regression from ever reaching a future deploy unnoticed again, because the team is no longer relying on remembering to re-audit this function by hand every time someone touches it -- the test does that automatically, on every single change, forever. The lesson underneath all three fixes is the same one: checks-effects-interactions ordering isn't a style preference auditors nitpick for the sake of it -- it's the literal, mechanical thing that determines whether a contract holding real money can be drained in a single transaction, and a test suite that only ever exercises normal wallets, however thorough, will never catch a bug that only a malicious contract can trigger. That's exactly the gap between lesson 13's clean rehearsal and lesson 15's confirmed exploit, closed for good.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Fixed claimRewards() by moving the rewardBalance zeroing before the external ETH transfer (checks-effects-interactions), added OpenZeppelin's ReentrancyGuard with nonReentrant as defense-in-depth, and moved Naomi's attacker-contract test from a one-off audit artifact into the permanent CI suite. Re-ran the exact exploit against the fixed contract -- it now reverts on the nested call while the attacker's own single legitimate claim still succeeds. Naomi re-audited and signed off; cleared for mainnet.

Naomi has re-verified and signed off.
